summary: An April Fools’ Day informational RFC (1 April 2019) from the Independent Stream. It satirically proposes four DNS record types, PASSWORD, CREDITCARD, SSN and SSNPTR, for storing customer data in public DNS. It is a joke about exposing sensitive information, not a real proposal.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8567 is an April 1st joke about putting passwords, credit card details, and Social Security information into DNS. It describes four record formats in a straight technical style to make the proposal's privacy problem clear.

subtitle: An April 1st joke proposes storing customer secrets in public DNS records.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke presents DNS as a place to keep customer identifiers and billing details for use by service providers.
tldr.mechanism: It describes four proposed DNS record types named PASSWORD, CREDITCARD, SSN, and SSNPTR, including their fields and formats.
tldr.outcome: The proposal is satire about placing sensitive customer information in DNS. The RFC's serious technical presentation is part of the joke.

today: RFC 8567 is an Informational April 1st document. Its proposed DNS record types are satire about storing sensitive customer data in a public naming system.

sections.title: The Satirical Proposal
sections.content: RFC 8567 proposes using DNS to store customer information for service-provider management. The introduction says customer information should be publicly accessible, and the document proceeds to specify four record types. It is an April 1st joke, not a serious proposal to publish customer secrets.
sections.plainLanguage: The document pretends that DNS should store personal customer details. This is an April 1st joke about exposing sensitive information.

sections.title: The Four Proposed Record Types
sections.content: The four record types are PASSWORD, for a username and password; CREDITCARD, for card and expiry information; SSN, for a Social Security number and birth date; and SSNPTR, which maps Social Security numbers to hostnames. RFC 8567 describes their wire formats and fields as if they were a practical standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The four names are PASSWORD, CREDITCARD, SSN, and SSNPTR. They describe fields for login details, payment details, personal identifiers, and reverse lookup.

sections.title: The Privacy Issue at the Center of the Joke
sections.content: The RFC says DNSSEC should be used with the proposed records to provide data integrity. Its premise is the joke: integrity does not remove the privacy problem created by placing sensitive customer data in DNS. The document's claims about sharing this data are satirical.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC discusses protecting these records from alteration. The deeper joke is that the records would expose private information in the first place.
